en: Dharmakīrti: *Hetubindu*. Homage to the Buddha.

(1.1) Since the comprehension of objects that are beyond the reach of the senses depends exclusively upon inference, this [treatise] is commenced in brief for the purpose of explaining that: "The logical reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds."
Because of the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), those others are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
(1.2) The "subject" (*pakṣa*) is the locus of the property (*dharmin*),
because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part.
If it is argued that this metaphorical usage is unjustified due to a lack of necessity, we say no.
Because the figurative usage has the purpose of negating both the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*), in this way visibility and so forth are avoided.

If it is argued that even by using the word "property" (*dharma*), since a property necessarily depends on something else, the very subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is established through proximity once the locus of the property is established—[we reply: no.
Because of proximity, the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) would also be included.

Once its existence in the subject of the example is established through the pervasion of that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), the further mention of the "subject" (*dharmī*) might be suspected of having the restrictive purpose of implying: "only that property which belongs to the subject of the example is the reason. Furthermore, although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, that existence is observed only in similar instances—is already established by the restriction [of the positive concomitance], the statement of non-existence in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve asattva*) [is made for the following reason].

Likewise here as well, although the existence [of the reason] in the subject of the example is established by the statement that it pervades a portion of that [subject], one might suspect that the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is intended to restrict its presence to that very [subject]. Therefore, even though the meaning is understood through the force of the context, the mention of the subject serves merely as a conventional designation for uniformity of expression, and thus the burden of comprehension is avoided. If it is argued: "If [the reason] is a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), then because it depends on that qualification, it does not extend elsewhere; thus, it would be an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason]," we say: No.
Because it is qualified by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
as in the case of "Caitra is an archer";
it is not by way of the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
As in the case of "Pārtha is an archer":
that which is a part of it is its property.
For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that [pervaded] is indeed the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) therein.
Or rather, it is the existence of the pervaded (vyāpya) in that very [locus].

By this, it is stated that both positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka), as well as the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), are ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

This is because, in every case of a reason, pervasion is not established through dissimilarity with the probandum (sādhyavaidharmya), or because there is no cessation [of the probandum] when the pervader (vyāpaka) has not ceased.
For the ascertainment of the pervasion by that property [the probandum] occurs through the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance.
In that regard, the presence of the property of the subject in the locus of the probandum is established either through direct perception or through inference;
as, for example, smoke in a particular location.
Or, [it may be] in the case of the property of being produced in sound.

For one who has perceived a location possessing smoke as having a form distinct from other objects—that is, by way of its unique (asādhāraṇa) nature—there arises a cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) which is based on memory and has as its object the particularity exactly as it was perceived.
In that process, it is precisely that initial perception whose object is the unique [particularity] that constitutes the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

(1.6) When that [object] has been seen in such a manner by perception, there arises a memory whose object is the exclusion of what is other (*atad-vyāvṛtti*), which expresses its uniqueness—that is, its distinction from whatever else is not unique to it.
This memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it functions through the power of perception;
it merely grasps the form exactly as it was perceived.
For one who, having previously perceived a unique object, expresses it as "unique," there is no apprehension of a new object;
moreover, since the means for accomplishing purposeful action was already seen by means of sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*),
that which was not previously seen cannot be cognized by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), just as in the case of inference.
For every discerning person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) investigates either a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or what is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

And a universal (*sāmānya*), which is apprehended by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) arising through the force of the perception of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), does not provide any purposeful action whatsoever—
unlike, for example, when one sees blue and has the cognition "this is blue."

For it is that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue which performs such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as the object to be accomplished; and that [characteristic] is indeed perceived by that very nature through the sensory perception (*ālocanā-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, the purposeful action to be accomplished by blue is not performed by the object of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of blue, which arises at a time subsequent to the apprehension of that particular characteristic.

(1.7) Therefore, even the definition that "a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object an unapprehended thing" must be qualified by the addition: "when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is unapprehended.

However, when the particular characteristic has already been apprehended, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising through the force of that [perception] and conforming to it is merely a form of memory (*smṛti*), because it has that [particular characteristic] as its object only in a derivative sense;
it is not a means of valid cognition.
Because that which has not yet attained the nature of a real entity cannot be apprehended;
because the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is based upon a real entity;
and because those who seek it act toward an object capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
For a real entity is characterized by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Even from that conceptual construction, a person acts toward the very entity itself through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it;
and because, upon such action, there is identity of purpose and result with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is argued that because the subsequent moments share the same functional efficacy (*yogakṣema*) as the preceding moment of direct perception, there would follow the consequence of invalidity for some of them, we say: no.
For when there is a desire for an object to be accomplished by a specific moment, their functional efficacy differs;
indeed, it is only regarding a common effect that there is no difference in their capacity.
Just as in the case of cognitions of inference regarding fire in general— such as when fire is closely proximate and inferred from various successive instances of smoke—

the validity of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) concerning the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), the mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, which arise subsequent to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is thereby refuted. Furthermore, in the case of an essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) consists in establishing the necessary connection (*anubandha*) of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) alone, because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is, in reality, of the same nature as that [proving property].
For that is the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the reason when it is applied to the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*).
For example: "Whatever exists is necessarily momentary;

because if there were non-momentariness, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be contradicted, and thus the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*), which is defined by that [efficiency], would be lost."

In the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), there is the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). This is as follows: when this [effect] is perceived, that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived; yet, even though other causes are present, it is not found in the absence of this [specific cause]. Thus, the existence [of the effect] when that [cause] exists and its non-existence when that is absent—which is established through direct perception and non-perception—is the causal relationship, and its establishment [constitutes the reason].

For the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) alone would thus apply to a distinct entity (*arthāntara*): "Wherever there is smoke, there is necessarily fire," because the existence of smoke occurs only when fire exists; that is what constitutes its being an effect.

In the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) as well, the determination of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) consists in establishing that the conventional usage of "non-existent" applies only to that which meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) yet is not perceived.
Because it demonstrates the absence of any other possible cause (1.9),

the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) occurs when, through the non-perception of the cause and the pervader— both of which have perceptible objects—

the relationship of cause and effect or pervaded and pervader has been established; this results in the proof of the absence [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum, by demonstrating the absence of the specified object.

Because the absence [of something] in a certain place cannot be established otherwise than through that which has reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), the demonstration of the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent—which has an unstated subject—succeeds only when the mere connection (*pratibandha*) is established. Therefore, in establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is no need to require the qualification of "having a perceptible object" for the two types of non-perception; for the ascertainment of negative concomitance consists in observing the non-observation of what exists and has reached the conditions for perception.
(1.10) This reason, characterized by these [definitions], is of exactly three kinds; it is of only three types:
essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
For example, when something is to be proven as impermanent, "existence" (*sattva*) [is used as a reason].
"Smoke exists in a place where there is fire," and "the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility when it is absent.
For it is precisely within these three types of reasons that the rule of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is established.
The pervasion of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as previously described is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

Since this does not exist elsewhere than in the three types of logical reasons (*hetu*), it is said to be restricted to these alone. (2.1) Among those, when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is such that its presence follows solely from the presence of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*), the reason is an essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Even though there is a difference in properties (*dharma*) due to the distinction between successive exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), in reality it is simply the nature of the mark (*liṅgasvabhāva*).

Since there is no deviation from the concomitance (*anvaya*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the very nature of the reason (*hetusvabhāva*), the qualification "by concomitance with that alone" (*tanmātrānvayena*) in the definition is made in consideration of the views of others. For others maintain that even a nature which has a different object as its cause and does not possess that [probandum's] state alone may still be a nature (*svabhāva*).
And by that qualification, he states that such [an entity] lacks that intrinsic nature (atatsvabhāvatā) and that the reason is inconclusive (vyabhicāra) with respect to that probandum;
for example, as in the case of "producedness" (kṛtakatva) with respect to a destruction that possesses a cause.
Its application is twofold.
One is by way of similarity (sādharmya) and the other by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
For example: "Whatever exists is all momentary, such as pots and so forth."
And sound is existent.
Likewise, in the absence of momentariness there is an absence of existence, and sound is existent.
Thus, the formal applications based on similarity and dissimilarity, characterized by the demonstration of pervasion through universal inclusion, have been stated.

(2.3) In this context, since the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is understood through the mere force of stating the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its relation [to the probandum], the employment of the proposition has not been demonstrated. If it is asked, "How can there be cognition of that [probandum] when the object of cognition (*prameya*) has not been demonstrated?"—
in one's own realization, who is there to demonstrate the object of cognition?

For one who has perceived smoke situated in a particular location, when there is a recollection of its pervasion by fire, the cognition of the meaning of the proposition "there is fire here" arises solely through the power of that [recollection]. Yet, in that case, no one informs him, "There is fire here," nor does he himself previously apprehend anything at all.
Since such a cognition occurs even without a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is useless due to the absence of a cause for its cognition.
What kind of sequence of cognition is this, whereby one first arbitrarily establishes that "fire is here" and subsequently resorts to an inferential mark to understand it?
Even if another person were to state it, it would merely float away, as it serves no purpose.
If it is argued that the "utility" [of perception] consists in the presentation of an object, then what is the purpose of that very object being presented?
If cognition could not otherwise occur, then everything would be acceptable.

Therefore, when this person cognizes by himself—even without some indicator that presents the object—he sees us as those who have a task to perform and clearly seeks a price, like a Brahmin at a festival.
Even from our words, he would cognize the probandum by following the logical mark (*liṅga*) which is already established for himself; so what difference is there between these two states?

Furthermore, since cognition is observed to occur even without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), through the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the connection [with the probandum] in an argument based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*), what is the use of it?
The proof (*sādhana*) is stated in order to produce a certainty in others that is identical to one's own certainty.

In this regard, what is the reason for resorting to a previously unheard-of sequence when one might lead another to understand [the truth] even without personally demonstrating the object of cognition (*prameya*)?
Therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the object of cognition, since understanding can arise even otherwise.
(2.4) By this, the introduction, conclusion, and so forth, are also refuted;
for the comprehension of the probandum is established by this much alone.
Abandoning your stubborn attachment, close your eyes and consider for a moment: does comprehension arise by this much, or not?
"What is the use of a proliferation of elaborations regarding the existence [of the probandum]?"—
thus, in a syllogism (*sādhana-vākya*), this much alone is the superior application.
(2.5) Herein, there is no fixed rule of sequence whatsoever that the reason (*hetu*) must be stated first and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) afterwards.
Because it is indicative in every respect.
(2.6) Even when the relation is explicitly stated, there is no difference in meaning whatsoever,
since in both cases it is precisely that state [of being] which is made manifest.

For when that which does not have the nature of another exists, there is no absolute existence of the other— just as when "being produced" exists, "being immediately subsequent to effort" may not. Likewise, even for an effect that does not have the nature of another, its absence does not entail the cessation of that [other], just as in these two cases, the cessation of one does not mean the cessation of the other.

Therefore, since even one of the two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—when employed according to its definition implies the second, the employment of both in a single proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*) is not desired, because it would be redundant.
For when positive concomitance is established by virtue of [the reason] being of that nature, the absence [of the reason] in the absence [of the probandum] is likewise established;
and when that is established, positive concomitance is also established.

Furthermore, the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not tenable even for the purpose of demonstrating a restriction—that the non-existence of the reason is manifested only in the absence of that [probandum], and not elsewhere, such as in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) or the contradictory instance;
for both the "other" and the "contradictory" are indeed dissimilar instances.
If it is asked: "How is this understood—that existence necessarily has a perishable nature—by virtue of which there could be the possibility of positive and negative concomitance?"
Because a cause for destruction is untenable,
entities are perishable by their very nature; once they have arisen from their own causes, their destruction does not arise from anything else,
because that [other cause] lacks efficacy.
For the cause of destruction does not produce the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, since that [nature] has already arisen from its own causes; nor does it produce a different entity,
because if a different entity were produced, the original entity would remain in its previous state, which would entail the consequence of its being perceived as such and so forth.
Nor is another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) its obscuration, because as long as that [nature] remains in its original state, an obscuration is impossible.
Nor is the non-existence of an entity produced by a cause of destruction;
for if non-existence were admitted as a positive entity (*vidhi*), it would inevitably fall prey to the dilemma of being either distinct or non-distinct [from the entity].

In the act of negating an entity, nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist. And thus, since there is no agent, there is no causality for a non-agent; therefore, there is no cause whatsoever for destruction.
Furthermore, [the notion of a cause for destruction] is redundant.
If an entity is perishable by its very nature and does not persist in itself, there is no need for causes of destruction,
because it perishes by its own nature alone.
For whatever has such a nature arises from its own cause as being exactly that way.
Furthermore, once that [nature] exists, it does not depend on another cause,

just like light, fluidity, heat, or solidity in a substance. For light and the others, having arisen as being of that very nature, do not subsequently depend on another cause for their state of being light and so forth.
For if there were no identity between that [nature] and the self, it would follow that there is no self at all.
Likewise, if an entity is established by its own nature as having the property of non-abiding, it does not require any further cause for that state of being identical to itself.
If it is argued that this is inconclusive because of the case of seeds and so forth—[meaning that seeds do not remain permanent despite their nature]—then [the response follows].

It might be argued that seeds and the like possess the intrinsic nature of producing sprouts and so forth, yet they do not produce them alone because they depend on other causes such as water; likewise, an entity might also require something else for its destruction. This is not so.
Because that which has such an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is produced, and that which lacks it does not have that intrinsic nature;
for this very reason, a difference between the entities in those two states must be determined.
Since there is no change in the intrinsic nature of things, it would follow that what has that intrinsic nature would be produced even before, just as it is afterwards.
Therefore, that which is the final specific state is itself the nature that produces the sprout;
however, the preceding specific states are the causes of the cause of the sprout, so there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason],
because among momentary entities, due to the arising of successive [states], there is an absence of identity.

(2.10) If those final [moments] are capable, why do they not produce [the effect] individually? They certainly do produce it; there is no other possibility here, because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-deviant. But if those auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) already possess a capable intrinsic nature, what further utility is there for another [cause]?
Indeed, entities possess no such capacity for deliberation that they might reflect, "Since this one among us is capable, what is there for us to do? and thereby desist from activity.
Having operations devoid of intention, their nature being such that they arise through the proximity of the transformation of their own causes, they do not deserve censure;
for such is their very nature.

If it is asked, "Are they not capable of producing one thing after another?"—no; because their capacity resides in that very [single effect], they are capable of producing only that one and nothing else, and thus there is no production of successive effects.

(2.11) If it is argued that when a single effect arises from auxiliary causes such as the eye and so forth, which possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), there would be no difference in the effect despite the difference in the causes—[we reply: no.

The application of those specificities [of causes] occurs according to their respective differences in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because through those applications there is no confusion regarding the specific natures of the effects.

For example, in the case of a jar produced from a lump of clay, a potter, a string, and so forth: its nature is distinct from trees and other things that do not have the nature of clay due to the lump of clay; and while it already possesses the nature of clay, it is distinct from all other things due to the potter, by virtue of having a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
The distinct nature of that very [pot], which consists of a particular configuration of clay, becomes differentiated from the wheel and other [causes] mentioned in the Sūtra.
Thus, in this way, the nature of the clay does not arise from the potter, nor does the particular configuration arise from the clay.

Nor, even though there is a difference in the objects of their respective specific potencies (*śaktiviśe�ṣa*), is there an essential difference in the effect produced by them due to a difference in those [potencies], because clay and shape are not identical with one another; for if they were, it would follow that they could not appear as distinct from the forms of "shape" and "clay.
If it is argued that shape is a quality entirely different from the substance of clay, and therefore the specific application of the potter and the lump of clay possess distinct natures—
It has been stated regarding this:
moreover, if shape were distinct from the clay, why does the potter not separate it?
Since a quality is dependent upon its substance, how could it be separated?

If that substance, which consists of the substratum for that configuration, exists by its very nature, or if that configuration consists of being supported by it, then why does it depend upon the activity of a potter? If this is asked, we reply: No.
Therefore, [the connection arises] from the attainment of mutual compatibility;

otherwise, if the lump of clay were by its very nature already compatible with such a configuration, then since the reality itself would possess the essential nature (*dharmatā*) characterized by compatibility even prior [to the production], it would follow that the connection with the specific configuration would already exist.
In that case, since that capacity arises in the clay substance from the potter, there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two;
for if there were a difference, the same consequences as before would follow.

Since it is established that even when there is a single intrinsic nature, one thing can possess specific qualities imparted by multiple conditions, why this excessive insistence on proving that clay and shape have a single intrinsic nature?

(2.13) Therefore, even though the effect possesses a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*) in reality, the auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) do not have a single object of utility. Just as here, due to the difference in causes and the application of distinct specificities, there is no single effect, so too should it be understood regarding the arising of consciousness from the eye and other [faculties].

To explain: from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is consciousness, the eye-consciousness derives its nature of apprehension (*upalambhātmatā*); and from that very same nature of apprehension...

From the sense organ of sight, there is the restriction of the capacity to grasp form; from the object, there is the corresponding form [of that cognition]. Thus, although the effect is in fact non-different [from its causes], distinct particularities arise precisely from the distinct natures of the various causes.
Therefore, even when there is a difference among the causes, there is no lack of differentiation in the particularity of their effect.

These very same distinct causal powers, being present with their capacities unimpeded for the production of their respective specific effects, are called the "basis for the persistence of the nature" of the effect of the totality (*sāmagrī*) because of their momentariness;

for indeed, from all those [causes] taken together, there arises a single, specifically characterized entity consisting of the apprehension of form—which is itself of the nature of perception—and the objective form.

In the case of momentary conditions whose powers are unobstructed, which produce immediate effects, and in which no further distinction can be added, what is the meaning of "cooperation" (*sahakāra*) among them?

Indeed, joint action does not consist everywhere in the production of an excellence; what then is it? It is the performance of a single purpose, even by many, as is the case with the final collection of causes.
That alone is the primary state of being an auxiliary for the auxiliaries, because that [final moment] alone possesses the status of a cause;
and at that moment, since it is impossible to produce a distinction due to the non-differentiation of the single nature.
Because the arising of a distinction is characterized by the production of another intrinsic nature,
its finality would be lost if it were to generate a further entity;
consequently, it could not be the direct cause.
Therefore, no excellence arises in the cause from its auxiliary conditions.

Those final conditions, which are momentary and by their very nature capable, arise together; they possess no prior, posterior, or separate existence, and from them the effect is produced immediately thereafter.
In this context, cooperation (*sahakāritva*) is simply the performance of a single purposeful action.
If it is asked, "From where does that which is capable arise?
[the answer is: from its own causes.
What do those [conditions] produce in him when they are in immediate proximity?
If it is argued that they might sometimes act otherwise, and thus even a single one might produce [the effect] somewhere, [we reply:

although the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), possessing distinct capacities at every moment through their connection with successive conditions, are perceived as similar due to some degree of uniformity as they continue in a stream, nevertheless, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed different.
Therefore, something is the cause of something else.
In that regard, the collection of form, sense faculties, and so forth, which exists in a location free from obstruction and other such conditions, is the cause capable of producing consciousness.
That specific condition (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*), which serves as the basis for their mutual approach and so on, is capable of producing that cause.

And since for these [factors] there is neither priority nor posteriority, nor a state of separateness, the defects that arise from priority, posteriority, and separateness do not apply even to those that are capable.
Therefore, whatever is the cause for their mutual approach and so forth is the cause of the capable [factor]; thus, in that regard, there is never any alteration.

(2.16) By this principle, the specific determination of the relation between cause and effect is to be seen everywhere with respect to capacities that follow a succession of distinct natures at every moment.
But this is not the case with entities that possess a stable, unitary nature, because a change in nature is impossible for them;

for it is logically untenable that the same entity could both possess the nature of being capable and incapable of action, such that it performs an action when accompanied by something else but does not perform it when alone.
If it is argued that "it acts when accompanied by another, but not when alone," [the response follows].
Is its nature incapable of producing an effect when alone?
If you say it is capable, why does it not produce it?
If it is asked, "How can he be capable if he does not act?"—if you argue that weavers and others, though capable of producing cloth and so forth, do not do so at all times; [we reply:
Your Majesty, who are fond of play and raised in luxury, causes even what has already been done to be done again and again.
For this has already been thoroughly examined by the statement "just like a seed, etc.
Therefore, since a change in intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is impossible, the persistence of that which possesses such a nature must be unavoidable, just as it is in its final state.
If, in the final state, capacity arises for that which was previously incapable, then that capacity—being of the very nature of the entity—is nothing other than its origination anew.
If it does not possess that intrinsic nature, then it is indeed a non-agent, because it is admitted that the effect arises from another entity called "capacity" (*sāmarthya*).
Furthermore, as for that [entity] which acts when all auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are present, why does it act only at that time?
We reply: it acts because it is observed acting.
Oh, how great is the power of the vision of the one of great majesty, since by its mere nature it employs even those things that do not possess such a nature in various kinds of activities!
If indeed anything were to somehow transcend the range of this venerable one’s vision,
alas, it would become something incapable of production and devoid of continuity— this thought torments the mind.

We certainly do not claim that entities which lack that [causal] nature perform an action simply by virtue of our seeing them; rather, those things possess the properties of cause and effect by their very nature.
We merely recognize them, upon seeing them, as having the nature of causal agents.
(2.18) This is indeed true.

Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in the property of performing an action; therefore, it would follow that all causal conditions (*pratyaya*) have failed in their duty if they do not perform the effect.
Is this intrinsic nature, which has the property of non-delayed activity, produced only at that final stage, or did it exist previously as well?
It existed [previously], because for those things whose nature is unchanging, unarisen, and stable, it is contradictory for any of their natures ever to be absent.
In that case, does it follow now that a woman is both a mother and a barren woman?
Or what is the meaning of this statement: "That which has the nature of non-delayed action does not produce its effect"?
If you argue that it possesses the nature of producing its own effect when combined [with other factors], but not when alone;
In that case, then, one [agent] would be alone and the other accompanied, due to a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
For a difference in intrinsic nature is indeed the defining characteristic of a difference in entities.
Indeed, even when in association, it could not be an agent by means of another's form.
And since its very nature remains exactly the same even prior [to the action], how could there ever be a cessation of activity?
Even for one for whom existence is momentary, why does it not act alone?
If it were so capable, it would certainly act.
How is it that [the self] does not exist?
Because of its momentariness.
It has been stated what kind of action belongs to such [a self].

How could that which exists in a single moment be otherwise? For that which comes into being is precisely that which does not [previously] exist; thus, this undesirable consequence does not apply, because there is a contradiction between the nature of an agent and a non-agent, and between that nature and its cause.
(2.20) Even for one who thinks: "Its very nature is the property of acting without delay," [the same fault remains].
That [cause] does not depend on association;
however, since the effect depends on other conditions, it arises only from those that are associated and not from them alone.
How then is it possible for that entity to produce [the effect] even when it is alone?
And since the effect does not arise from that [agent], the contradiction remains as it was.
If you argue that the agent does not merely act alone,
then how can it have the nature of non-delayed action?
Is it not the case that this very point has been illuminated: that he indeed acts?
And how could he, being capable even when alone, disregard another who is dependent upon him for the effect?
Disregarding this [objection] entirely, one should proceed by force;
for in this way, its own capacity is demonstrated.
You state that an effect depends upon another, and thus it does not arise from that [cause] alone; yet you also say that it is capable in its solitary state, and therefore it does arise from it.
And how could these two [the cause and the effect] be thus?
Therefore, this person, whose vital points are being pierced by the thorn of envy, merely deserves to be ignored as he wails in distress.
Consequently, this state of cooperation, characterized by the performance of a single purposeful action, belongs only to momentary entities.

But this does not apply to non-momentary things, for those whose existence is possible even separately— since it is impossible for them to have a fixed rule of cooperation given the possibility of producing their effects individually.
However, in cases where entities attain the status of causes through the assistance of a continuum (*santāna*),
such as fire, water, and earth in the production of boiled rice and sprouts from rice seeds and the like;

In this context, the "cooperative action" (sahakriyā) of conditions is said to consist in the production of a specific quality (viśeṣa) based on the continuum (saṃtāna), not based on a substantial entity (dravya),
because no specific quality can arise within a momentary substance.
For if no specific quality were produced in rice and the like, there would be no production of cooked rice even when fire and other factors are present.

Likewise, for one who has entered a dark room from a bright space, if the sense faculty did not acquire a gradual excellence (*atiśaya*) from its own auxiliary factors, then it would not produce the apprehension of an object at all, just as before;
for among the sense faculties and so forth, which act without delay, no production of a specific quality (*viśeṣotpatti*) is possible through mutual interaction.

In that case, those [factors] which have reached a state of suitable location and so forth—based on their respective conditions and their mutual approach—attain the status of being causes of cognition simultaneously with the perfection of their own nature; thus, there is indeed only a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).

Cooperation (sahakāritvam). However, where the auxiliary conditions (pratyaya) produce a specific quality, there the causal continuum depends upon other conditions; thus, there is the acquisition of a different intrinsic nature (svabhāvāntara). In that case, when the preceding moments of the causal conditions cease by their own inherent force (svarasataḥ), from those very [conditions] arises a distinguished moment. In this manner, it proceeds step by step until, from the final assemblage of causes possessing extreme excellence, [the result is produced].
The production of the effect:

(2.23) If the effect were produced from a causal factor that has acquired a particularity through auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), then the production of that very particularity itself would not occur.
If a particularity were to arise from what is undifferentiated [from its cause], then the effect itself would likewise [arise from it].
Consequently, the auxiliary causes would produce the effect without depending on the production of mutual distinctions among themselves;
thus, even non-momentary entities could possess causal efficacy when dependent upon auxiliaries,
and there would be no arising of any excellence in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) from those things upon which they depend.

Now, if it were to arise only as something that has already acquired a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) for the sake of producing a particular excellence conducive to the arising of the effect through its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*),
then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, the auxiliary causes do not remain in a state of constant fitness for producing the mutual excellences conducive to the arising of the effect.
If it is argued that there must be some constant adjunct (*nityānuṣakta*) by which a distinction (*viśeṣa*) arises among these [causes],
because we observe the production or non-production of an effect depending on the presence or absence of that [adjunct],
and therefore this initial distinction does not arise for something that receives no assistance from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Furthermore, we feel no distress even at being told this repeatedly, provided that through such means the world may attain an understanding of the correct principle.
Well then, let it be said:
the status of being a "cooperative cause" for cooperative factors is not possible in an ultimate sense by virtue of producing a distinct [effect].

For, in the absence of that [distinction], there would be a lack of auxiliary cooperation when a distinction is to be produced. (2.24) Now, how could even the performance of a single purposeful action occur? That too would not occur for those things which are devoid of mutual distinction.
If it were to occur, [it would be so without a cause].
It might also exist separately;
and if it were so, then the effect, which by nature arises from that specific quality, would also arise from the cause alone.
To this, the following answer has been stated: just as a specific quality arises within the continuum of an entity through various successive conditions at every moment.

The specific states such as being in a suitable location and so forth possess the capacity for causal efficiency; and from these [states] arises [the effect], yet even though each possesses its own power, there is no action when they are isolated.

Because there is no separate, individual existence for each specific agent, the twofold nature of the effect— and likewise the distinction between cause and effect regarding their intrinsic natures— is explained as being like that of the sense faculties and consciousness acting without delay through their co-operating conditions (*sahakārin*). (2.25) In that regard, when an effect arises from co-operating conditions in dependence upon the assistance to the continuum, the initial particularity (*viśeṣa*) of the co-operating conditions does not arise from a particularity produced by those co-operating conditions themselves.

Just as with an immediate effect, those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that arise from it are produced by it because they have it as their material cause (*tatprakṛtitva*); thus, there is no infinite regress.
Likewise, if even a non-momentary entity (*akṣaṇika*) produces an effect, [it does so through such a causal process].
Granted that he acts;
however, if his nature were such that he acts without delay, then it has been stated that since a separate existence is possible, he would likewise act even when alone.
But that which does not possess that nature remains non-productive even then.

Therefore, for non-momentary causes, there is no rule of cooperation based on the performance of a single purposeful action, nor is there one based on assistance through a causal series; thus, nothing can be its auxiliary, and it would produce the effect even when alone.

Generally, however, a continuum of entities (*bhāva-santāna*) that exists as an aggregate is seen to perform its own effect when it has acquired specific qualities produced by auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), just like a seed and so forth.

For one who maintains the doctrine of a permanent cause, there must clearly be the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*) in the cause which acts in dependence upon other conditions.
If the causal nature were already present even previously, its non-activity would be illogical.

(2.26) Therefore, whatever has a certain nature exists as such by its mere existence; it does not come to be that way after having been otherwise, nor does it depend on the further conditioning of another for that state. Thus, for an entity whose nature is non-abiding, there is nothing to be effected by causes of destruction. Likewise, even for an entity whose nature is abiding, there is nothing to be effected by causes of destruction, because it is impossible for anyone to bring about a change in its intrinsic nature.

If there were the apprehension of its becoming otherwise, it would not possess that very nature; thus, the same alternative as before would apply. And the refutation of that has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, that which is a state of being otherwise due to another is a different nature; and how could that which is different belong to it?
For a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the defining characteristic of a difference in entity (*vastu*).
And thus, for that which has arisen with the property of stability, there could be no alteration of state (*anyathābhāva*).
By this, the production of a different intrinsic nature—such as liquidity—in copper and other substances through fire and so forth, when they possess solidity and other qualities, is refuted.
In that case as well, because the preceding [entity] ceases by its own inherent nature, another entity with a nature such as liquidity arises from the fuel of fire and so forth;
for it is produced by its own causes as something whose very character is stability, since it would persist if a cause of destruction were absent. (2.27)
If it is argued that its destruction occurs from something else,
and that destruction is not a separate intrinsic nature (svabhāva), but rather destruction is simply the departure of the entity itself; [then we reply:]
This does not transcend the following two alternatives: is the entity eternal, or is it non-eternal?

Furthermore, by asserting that "having first been eternal, it subsequently becomes non-eternal," one speaks of a duality of entities—a distinction between the natures of the eternal and the non-eternal.

By stating that the previously intended eternal nature itself perishes, one asserts both destruction and non-destruction at all times; thus, in the former case, a cause for destruction is simply ineffective.
It does not become impermanent after having previously been permanent;
rather,
it remains precisely permanent even afterwards.
Because it possesses a single nature.
In that case, how can that entity be said to have perished if it does not enter into destruction by way of its own nature?
For the entity and the destruction of its nature are not of a mutually identical form.
Therefore, if destruction were real, that [destruction] would have to possess the nature of destruction;
nevertheless, it has been stated that the cause of destruction is thus useless.
Consequently, whether an entity is by its own nature perishable or imperishable, there is no utility for a cause of destruction.

(2.28) Therefore, since an entity is independent with respect to its destruction, it is necessarily subject to that [destruction]. Thus, "whatever exists is perishable," and upon the cessation of perishability, there is the cessation of existence; this establishes the proof of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). If it is argued: "Even if perishability were inherent by nature (*svabhāva*), something might still exist that does not possess that nature. For it is not the case that everything is the nature of everything; therefore, the proof of positive and negative concomitance based on that [inherent nature] is not established."
No, for if it were non-momentary, it would follow that it lacks reality;
for capacity is the defining characteristic of an entity,
whereas the absence of all capacity is the defining characteristic of a non-entity.
Furthermore, that which is non-momentary possesses no efficacy whatsoever, because it lacks the capacity for causal activity either successively or simultaneously.
Thus, the pervasion is established: whatever exists is necessarily momentary.
(3.1) When another object is to be understood, the effect is a logical reason because it is non-deviant.

If it were argued that, since the capacity to indicate [the probandum] exists through the relation of cause and effect, the relationship of the indicated and the indicator would exist in all respects—because the relationship of the produced and the producer exists in all respects—the answer is: no.
Because, in the absence of that [cause], there would be no necessity for the arising of those [effects].
Therefore, an effect is the logical reason (*hetu*) for as many essential natures (*svabhāva*) as it is invariably concomitant with in its cause,
because of the necessity of its being an effect of that cause.
If it is argued that there would be a partial relationship of produced and producer with respect to those very factors without which [the effect] does not exist,
we say no; for this is accepted when one grasps the specific qualities produced by them, as is the case with universals that have specific marks as their limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
If one intends to refer to the general [property] without qualification, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and thus its capacity to indicate (*gamakatva*) is not accepted.

If it is argued: "Even if something exists for someone at some time due to some cause, how is it determined that everything of that kind has such an origin? And in that case, there would be neither positive nor negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."
No, because that which does not arise from it would never arise from it even once.
Cause and effect are characterized by the nature of producer and produced in mutual dependence.

In this regard, if smoke were to arise from something other than the causal complex of fire and so forth, then its nature would not be produced by that [complex], and thus it would not arise from it even once.
It is like a different object;
nor could a causal complex produce it, because its nature is not that of producing such a thing,
just like any other causal complex.
Furthermore, it is not logical for smoke to have a nature that is both produced by that [cause] and not produced by it,
because it would possess a single nature.
If it were to arise from a nature that produces both smoke and non-smoke, it would consequently possess the nature of both smoke and non-smoke.

Because the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of effects are produced by the intrinsic natures of their causes, and because it would follow that things would be causeless if they did not depend on causes; therefore, that which produces smoke is a specific causal complex consisting of fire and so forth, and that which is produced by that specific causal complex of fire and so forth is precisely smoke. Thus, there is a restriction of the intrinsic nature of cause and effect in this manner.
There is no production from that which is of a different class. Whatever kind of effect has been observed once to arise from whatever kind of cause, that [effect] does not deviate from it.
Thus, when the causal relation is established, the pervasion of the effect by the cause is established.
(3.3) But surely it is observed that some things arise even from heterogeneous causes, as for example, lotus stalks and the like from cow dung and so forth.
[Reply: There is no production from the heterogeneous.
For precisely such a thing is the primary cause of those [lotuses]; thus, there is no difference in the cause.
In the case of a continuous process (*prabandha*), however, [the distinction] arises from the source;
for there exists a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between that which is born from cow dung and that which is not, even though their form (*rūpa*) is identical.
Indeed, the mere similarity of appearance is not the sole cause for the identity of entities.
For even among certain things that possess an identical form, a distinction between their classes is observed due to some other specific difference.

Otherwise, if an undifferentiated effect were produced from a differentiated causal complex, then the differentiation and non-differentiation of effects would not follow from the differentiation and non-differentiation of causes; consequently, the differentiation and non-differentiation of the entire universe would be causeless.
For it would follow that there is no differentiation from differentiation, nor non-differentiation from non-differentiation.
Furthermore, since there would be no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities distinct from that [cause], entities—being without a cause—would either exist eternally or not exist at all.
For it is through dependence that entities are occasional;
moreover, there would be no systematic application of means to the ends to be accomplished.
For, if the causal capacity were restricted, only a specific thing would be employed as the means to accomplish something, and not anything else,
because that [specific thing] alone possesses the capacity for it.
Furthermore, because another [cause] lacks that capacity, those two are distinct by virtue of having natures consisting respectively of producing that [effect] and not producing it.

Even if that [effect] were to arise from something whose nature is different from the nature of producing it, there would be no restriction regarding the power to produce it; consequently, anything could arise from just anything.
However, if there is an equality in the power to produce it, then it is indeed that very [cause]; thus, the effect does not deviate from its cause.
(4.1) The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension is the cause for the absence [of an object] or for the conventional usage regarding its absence.
In this context, since apprehension is a property of the apprehending subject, apprehension is the cognition thereof.
Therefore, the apprehension of something else is "non-apprehension," because it is other than the intended apprehension.
It is by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), like [the avoidance of] things that are unfit to be eaten or touched.
When something possesses the nature of being perceived, its "perception" (*upalabdhi*) is the objective essence characterized by the capacity to produce a cognition of its own object;
for this capacity is the very nature of the entity itself.

Therefore, as before, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is simply that which is capable of producing apprehension of something else. When one thing is being apprehended, the apprehension of another necessarily occurs because there is no difference in their capacity for apprehension; they are conjoined with it due to their association within a single cognition (*ekajñāna*).
For if both were present, a cognition restricted to only one form would be impossible.

Therefore, since those two possess an identical capacity for being associated within a single cognition, it is their mutual dependence that is intended here as "otherness," by virtue of relying upon proximity.
If that [cognition] alone is called "other" in relation to that [object], then that cognition or its own nature constitutes the non-perception characterized by the knower and the known.
It establishes either the absence of the counter-positive or the conventional usage of "absence.

If it is asked: "How can the existence of another thing be the absence of that [specific thing], such that the non-perception of a positive entity could establish either an absence or the conventional usage of 'absence'?"—it has been stated in this regard that, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), that object distinct from it, or the cognition thereof, is called "absence" or "non-perception" due to its dependence on such a [negative] reference.
It is not a mere negation,
because that would entail the impossibility of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence due to the lack of proof for it.

Since the establishment of one entity in its unassociated form is itself the establishment of the non-existence of another, the existence of something else is designated as the non-existence of that [other].

Whether non-existence characterized by the presence of another thing is established by itself as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thereby establishes the conventional usage of that non-existence,

or whether it is established by the establishment of that [other thing], there is no distinction whatsoever such that there would be a contradiction in establishing the conventional usage of non-existence through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Why then should that very presence of another thing and the apprehension directed toward it not be the proof of that non-existence?
If it is asked, "Is the establishment of non-existence itself the establishment of that absence?
[the answer is] no, because there is no separate establishment and because there is an absence of a relationship;
for the existence of something else is not the means of proof here.
When the establishment of one thing does not entail the establishment of another, the latter serves as the logical mark (liṅga) for the former, as in the case of smoke and fire.
The absence of a thing is established precisely through the establishment of the existence of something else;
for the exclusion of other things is established by that very means of valid cognition which determines the reality of that [object] whose nature is unmingled with others.
(4.4) Furthermore, because of the absence of a relationship: if that [mark] were to be the indicator (*liṅga*) of that [object], there would have to be some kind of relationship between the two.

For example, there is the inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) between "being produced" and "impermanence," or the inherence in a single substrate with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) in the case of smoke.

Neither the relationship of container and contained nor the relationship of producer and produced exists between existence and non-existence; there is no such connection by which the existence of another thing could serve as its proof.
If it is argued that there is a subject-object relationship, like the relationship between a word and its meaning:

If there were an intention to convey that [meaning] by means of both the word and the object, their relationship would have to be characterized either as cause and effect or as inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
However, neither of these is possible here; rather, there must be a relationship of subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).
For it is only when the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhya-sādhanabhāva*) between the two is established that the relationship of subject and object can occur through that medium.
And that very [non-existence] is not established in the absence of a relationship;
otherwise, this would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, if non-existence were established through the existence of another thing, then the non-aggregate (*asamudāya*) would be what is to be proven.
And if it were the case that "the absence of a jar [is established] because of the presence of something else," it would follow that the jar is absent everywhere and at all times.

This is not so; for a locus such as a specific place is qualified by the absence of the jar, and thus it is this absence, acting as a qualifier of that locus, that is being proved, not the absence in its isolation.
Therefore, it is not the case that a non-composite entity is what is being proved.

If it is argued that there is no lack of connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), because the presence of another (*anyabhāva*) is connected with a location (*pradeśa*) and so forth,
we say no; for the location and so forth are themselves the presence of another.
For in whatever place or location it is said that "it exists," that very thing is the "presence of another" (*anyabhāva*) unconnected with it.

Since the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "the jar is not here" arises precisely from the perception of that [other presence], how could there be a relationship of sign and signified (*liṅgaliṅgibhāva*) between those two?

(4.6) Furthermore, the postulation of a relationship of universal and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) is not possible here, by which the universal might be the reason (*hetu*) and the particular the property (*dharma*).
Since the non-existence of that [object] is cognized precisely through the cognition of its specific absence,
it cannot function as a logical reason (*hetu*) because it lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) elsewhere and because it would constitute a mere part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that wherever there is merely a location, there is the absence of a jar.
If it is argued that there is an absence everywhere in such a solitary place, [we reply]:
surely its very solitude is the absence of the jar; and since that [solitude] is established only through the cognition of that [absence], of what, then, is that now the logical mark (*liṅga*)?
The pursuit of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is likewise pointless.
Therefore, the existence of another thing (*anyabhāva*) is not a means of proving non-existence (*abhāva*).
If it is argued that there is a relationship of contradiction (*virodha*), and that non-existence is established from the existence of another thing on that basis;

With what is there a contradiction for what by means of the existence of another? Indeed, why would the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) be intended to be cognized such that there could be a relationship of contradiction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)?
The non-existence of the counter-positive, the jar, is not contradicted by the existence of another, because they can coexist.
Since that [non-existence] is the object of cognition (*prameya*), how could there be a contradiction between the mark and the possessor of the mark?
Therefore, there is an absence of a relationship.
In this case as well, the fact that it is not established by a collection remains as it was.

(4.8) If it is argued: "But surely, if there were no relationship between the existence of another thing and its own non-existence, then even through the cognition of the existence of another thing, there would be no cognition of its non-existence."

Indeed, it is not accepted that the existence of another thing indicates the absence of a given thing on the basis of some relationship; rather, the existence of another thing is itself its absence, as stated previously.

For that which is of an unmingled nature—existing alone and established in its own singular essence—the very determination of it in its own form is the exclusion of the other. Since the isolation of that [thing] is precisely the deficiency of the other, the existence of the one is itself the absence of the other.
Consequently, the apprehension of that very thing is itself the non-apprehension of anything other than it.
Otherwise, if by the determination of that [thing] nothing other than it were excluded, there would be no such determination of it at all,
because there would be no distinction between that which possesses its own nature and that which does not.
Whatever worldly convention exists for someone, in a certain place, based on observation for the purpose of attaining or avoiding something—that would not be possible.
For even one who sees fire does not see *only* fire; how then would a seeker of water not proceed toward it?
If it is argued that the absence of water is cognized through non-perception (*anupalambha*), [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "non-apprehension"?
If it is the absence of the apprehension of water, then how can an absence be the cognition of anything, or the cause of a cognition? And how can there even be a cognition of that [absence] itself?

If non-existence were perceived even when there is no cognition of that [object] or of anything else, then why would it not also be perceived during states such as sleep, intoxication, fainting, or being turned away?
This has already been examined in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.
Therefore, even while seeing fire, one who does not determine "this is fire" would neither stay nor remain there.
And from that, there would follow for the one who perceives it an insurmountable calamity.

(4.9) If you argue that the comprehension of the non-existence of the other arises precisely from the perception of the one, how does the perception of one thing cause one to understand that the other exists elsewhere?
If you say it is because of the perception of that one thing alone—
Why does this which we have already stated earlier appear harsh to you?
Therefore, like a bird that cannot see the shore, one must return even after wandering far; enough with this pursuit of directions that lack any foundation.
(4.10) If the exclusion of others were established by the mere determination of one thing, then the non-existence of everything else would be established there without distinction.
But it does not apply only to that which is in an equivalent state of being perceptible.
Furthermore, the qualification "the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is the means of proving non-existence" need not be stated,
because even those things that have not reached the conditions for perception are excluded from that [context].

(4.11) Through the determination of its own nature, there occurs the exclusion of other natures, because cognition has an appearance restricted to that nature; for the nature of one thing cannot be the nature of another.
Otherwise, as previously argued, there would be an absence of both engagement and withdrawal if there were no exclusion of other natures.
And the intellect, perceiving that [object] as restricted by place, time, intrinsic nature, and state through its own nature, thereby excludes any deviation from that state.

For in this way, that [object] becomes determined and delimited by its specific place and so forth, provided that its being otherwise is excluded; and since suchness belongs to that very thing and not to another, it delimits that which is thus-become precisely by excluding what has become otherwise.
In this manner, the operation of a single means of valid cognition establishes all entities within two categories.
For it is precisely by generating the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that [the means of knowledge] achieves its purpose.
Since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established solely through the exclusion of everything other than that [subject], the absence of any other mode [of proof] is proven.

For if there were no pervasion because it were other than that, then by virtue of being other, it would not exclude the object in question; consequently, there would again follow the undesirable consequence of the entity remaining unascertained.

(4.12) Therefore, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates upon something, it determines that object, excludes what is other than it, and indicates the absence of a third possibility; thus, this is the single operation of one means of valid cognition.
For instance, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates upon a certain object, it excludes that very object from what is other than itself, because it determines that very object;
and it excludes what is other than that [object] from it, because it does not determine anything else therein.

Therefore, that very means of valid cognition establishes the absence of any other mode [of existence], because everything is established as being either perceived within it or as being other than it, and because only that which is not other than it is established as being that very thing.
By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth—which consist of mutual exclusion—are also explained.
Thus, from the perception of one thing, there is the exclusion of that which is of a nature other than it;
however, there is no exclusion of everything else that exists in its place or at its time.
Therefore, it must be both non-identical with that [object] and yet occupy its same space and time,
like taste, color, and so forth. Consequently, from the aforementioned non-perception itself, the non-existence of something, somewhere, and at some time is established.
(4.13) Even the perception of another existing thing is accepted as establishing that non-existence, but not by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For even in that case, since there is no relationship [between the two], the situation is the same regarding the non-existence being a separate probandum;
moreover, the non-existence is established at the very moment the logical mark manifests.
For one does not, having apprehended the existence of another thing, establish its positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and thereby apprehend its non-existence.
What then? One apprehends its non-existence precisely while apprehending that which is other than it, because immediately after perception one establishes: "this exists, but this does not exist."
And that alone constitutes its logical mark (liṅga) which possesses both positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Since the examples are unestablished, it is not possible to demonstrate in this way: "wherever there is the perception of the existence of another thing, there is the absence of that [first] thing."

Because the apprehension of that [object] alone does not occur anywhere; and when demonstrating by way of generality, there is no other means of valid cognition even in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), but rather that very apprehension of the existence of something other than it is what establishes the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Thus, there is an infinite regress of examples, which results in a lack of comprehension.
Therefore, the non-existence of that [object] cannot be established by any logical mark whatsoever.

That "existence of another" (anyabhāva), being established through non-apprehension characterized as perception, may bring about the conventional usage of "non-existence" for the sake of a confused person's understanding; enough with this digression.
(4.14) This non-apprehension is thus threefold.
When the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established, there is the non-perception of a cause whose absence is established;

and when the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is established, there is the non-perception of a pervader whose absence is established, as well as the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
In those cases, even the conventional usage of the absence of a cause or a pervader is established only through the establishment of the presence of something other than them.
Having been established in that manner, it proves the absence of the effect and the pervader, or the conventional usage of "absence.

However, in the case of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the conventional usage of "absence" itself is proved by means of non-perception acting as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

(4.15) If [the reason is] the cause or the pervader, then through the establishment of the existence of something other than them, non-perception establishes both the absence of the other and the conventional usage of its absence.

And since that [non-apprehension] is the establisher of the conventional designation of non-existence only when the two [objects] have reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), how could there be an application of it regarding an object that is beyond perception (*parokṣa*)?
It is not an application as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not certain.

For it is solely for the purpose of demonstrating that when the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—whose relations are already established—are absent, the other [the effect or the pervaded] must necessarily be absent as well, that these two [types of evidence] are employed.

This very property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekavat*), is pervaded by a portion of that [subject]; thus, the three-fold reason alone, possessing the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), is the indicator because it does not deviate from its own probandum-property (*svasādhyadharma*).
Others, however, maintain that the reason has six characteristics (*ṣaḍliṅga*).
And these three [characteristics] are: having an uncontradicted object, having the intended singular number, and being known.
Among these, "having an uncontradicted object" is not a separate characteristic, because there is a contradiction between contradiction (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
For inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) means that the reason exists only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists.
That reason, possessing such a characteristic, would exist in the subject (*dharmin*); and in this case, how could the property to be proven not be present there?

Indeed, when perception and inference subvert the property to be proven, they expel it from the subject; yet, while that [property] exists, the reason—by existing only when it exists—establishes it right there. Oh, what a state of instability for entities!
If you say that the reason (*hetu*) must be inseparably connected (*avinābhāvī*) with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), but not necessarily with the subject (*sādhyadharmī*);
then is this poor fellow, having married a eunuch, now searching for a son?
For [in such a case], the reason would exist even when the property to be proven is absent from the subject.
Having pointed that out, how can it be said that "that subject possesses the property to be proven"?
For this very reason, the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) has been stated.

It might be argued: since the reason could otherwise be [unestablished], for that very reason the subject is said to be one whose property is not sublated by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What, then, is the efficacy of the reason (*hetu*) now? If the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the mere absence of sublation (*abādha*), the reason is useless.
Even in the case of sublation, since the absence of the probandum is established by it [the reason], how can there be any efficacy in the means of proof?

If there were no restriction, then when a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) operates against the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), the absence of that subverting proof would entail the possibility of the absence of the probandum; thus, non-subversion (*abādhā*) lacks logical force.
Non-subversion is not simply the absence of subversion.

What then? It is the non-perception of sublation (*bādhā*). And since that [non-perception] might occur for a person even when sublation is possible in some cases, it is the proper domain for the employment of a logical reason (*hetu*). Why indeed would a reason fear the perception of sublation rather than sublation itself, such that—disregarding sublation—it is desired to be employed only upon its non-perception? In that case, should it not be employed upon the non-perception of sublation while disregarding, in the ultimate sense, whether sublation exists or does not exist?
For what purpose is it employed?
It is for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*).

Could it be that this [probans] might establish the probandum even when some sublation (*bādhā*) is present, such that no effort is made to ascertain its absence and the probans is nevertheless employed?
This being the case, "having a non-sublated object" cannot be a defining characteristic of a logical reason (*hetu*),
because its capacity remains effective even when sublation exists.
Furthermore, under such circumstances, the engagement of one who is in doubt would not be justified.

Just as one employs [a reason] even when no sublation is perceived—having accepted that [non-perception]—so too should one employ it when sublation is perceived, for there is no difference in the acceptance [of the reason].
If it is argued that "the reason lacks efficacy when sublation exists," [we reply: no.

If this is so, then a reason that has not had the possibility of sublation determined is fit for formal application, lest there be a lack of capacity even for a reason that has been applied when sublation is possible.
If it is argued that there is capacity provided there is no perception of sublation;
Does perception pervade sublation,
such that the incapacity of a reason caused by the impossibility of sublation would not occur? Or rather, does sublation cease when that [perception] ceases?

Nevertheless, because the probandum is not established simply due to the non-perception of sublation (*bādhā*), the logical reason (*hetu*) is futile; for as long as there is no perception [of sublation], sublation is impossible.
Even if perception ceases, if sublation does not cease, the incapacity of the reason remains as it was; thus, it is not a valid application (*aprayoga*).

Therefore, since a reason that exists otherwise than by being superimposed upon the presence or absence of its own probandum does not bring about anything nor cause anything to cease in the locus (*dharmin*), its presentation is ineffective.
Thus, there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); in this regard, non-sublation constitutes another essential form [of the reason].

(5.5) In that case, there would have to be another qualification for that [absence], and it would deserve to be stated as a separate definition, such that even when one exists, the other might be absent—just as, for example, "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and "presence in the similar class" (*sapakṣe bhāvaḥ*).

And since this [absence] is not possible when there is non-contradiction (*abādhā*) given the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), sublation (*bādhā*) cannot occur in the domain of the contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*), which are invariably concomitant with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*). Therefore, its absence is not a separate definition distinct from these two.
This must be stated: therefore, when the reason (*hetu*) is employed, there is no possibility of faults in the thesis (*pratijñā*);
nor is the thesis ever employed in isolation.

Consequently, defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) need not be mentioned. (5.6) By this, the intention to express [the reason] as a singular number is also refuted. How so? For a single reason would exist only in the presence of its own probandum; it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*) only there. Therefore, how could anything other than that also be a reason for that same [probandum]?
That which is to be proven for one [reason] exists only when there is the presence of a property that does not subvert it; thus, it is the same as [the case of] subversion.

(5.7) Furthermore, is that which is in reality incapable of having a counter-reason intended as the cause of either correct knowledge or its opposite, or is it one for which a counter-reason has not been demonstrated? What follows from this?
If it is one for which a counter-reason is impossible, then because it is impossible to ascertain [its status], this is not a defining characteristic, or rather, it is a non-reason (*ahetu*).

For a property that serves as a means of proof (*pratipādaka-dharma*) cannot possess the character of being a valid reason (*tallakṣaṇatva*) if its own nature is not certain, just as the presence of a property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is not valid when it is itself doubtful.
