Nor could a reason have a doubtful character; otherwise, no reason would exist at all.

Since the possibility of a counter-instance (*pratiyogin*) is observed in cases where the characteristics are identical, this suspicion arises even regarding those cases where no counter-instance has been seen, because there is no distinction between them.

Or, if there is a distinction, that distinction must be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the reason (*hetu*), because through that distinction the reason—being entirely free from opposition (*nirasta-pratipakṣa*)—ascertains its own probandum (*svasādhya*). Thus, that which lacks such a characteristic would not be a valid reason; and in that case, the intention to specify [the reason] as being "one" in number would be useless.

Consequently, the definition of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) would be lost, for the "non-erroneous contradictory" is defined as occurring when two reasons, each possessing its own specific characteristic, fall into conflict within a single locus (*dharmin*).
(5.8) Furthermore, the specific nature of that particularity has not been pointed out, such that by means of its form we might perceive the possibility or impossibility of a counter-correlative.
Therefore, one must entertain doubt everywhere that such a particularity does not exist at all.
Even in the case of a reason for which a counter-reason has been observed, no distinction whatsoever is perceived from other [reasons] prior [to that observation];
nor is there always the perception of such a counter-reason even when one is possible. However, superior wisdom is seen to be capable of conceiving a counter-reason.
Therefore, in reality, there is no certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of a counter-thesis (*pratiyogin*).
Since the characteristic of being a potential counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is itself uncertain, no reason at all would be valid.
(5.9) Now, as for one who has not presented a counter-reason, as it has been said:

“If, then, one accepts that ‘sound-ness’ (*śabdatva*) is eternal, then this [reason] would indeed be a valid reason, provided that no one were to point out the reason for impermanence, such as ‘being produced’ (*kṛtakatva*), in this case. Now, a very great calamity has arrived; because it was stated by our teachers, it ought not to be made public, yet since we must uphold the principles of logic (*nyāya*), it cannot be concealed—how can this most grievous calamity be endured?

This reason, having first established entities as being of the nature of its own probandum and having joined the persons who rely on those [entities] with worldly prosperity and the supreme good, is then— by a person possessed of ingenuity, through the demonstration of another reason— rendered powerless in its proof; it thereby causes those entities to fall away from their perfection of that state, and those persons to fall away from their perfection of worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
"What can we say to this—that he goes to the forest of asceticism like a king who has lost his kingdom?
(5.10) For if the status of being a means were produced by human ingenuity, then nothing would be either a means or a non-means.
And if that reason, by its very nature, possesses that property, how could it be made otherwise?"
Because there is no alteration of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity,
and because a single thing cannot possess two contradictory natures;
and how could that which does not possess the property [of the probandum] at one time ever be a means of proof (*sādhana*) for anything at another time?

Therefore, since a counter-reason possessing those same characteristics is impossible for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)— which by their very nature are inseparable from their respective probanda and possess the aforementioned definitions— the intention to state them as a single number lacks a defining characteristic, because there is nothing to be excluded [from that category]. Furthermore, since cognition is not the intrinsic form of the logical mark (*liṅga*), how could it constitute a definition of the logical mark?
When considering from what kind of reason (*hetu*) the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is to be known, the nature of the non-deceptive mark (*liṅga*) for the cognizer is stated;

upon seeing which, one establishes the means of proof (*sādhana*) through its specific differentiation, and based on the conviction that it brings about the presence of the desired object, one undertakes purposeful activity.
Likewise, that which constitutes its own nature (ātmarūpa) is its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), but not the nature of another.

If being a defining characteristic were based merely on utility at the time of the arising of cognition, then even objects of knowledge such as a person (puruṣa) would become defining characteristics;
for even in their absence, there would be no cognition of the subject possessing the mark (liṅgin).
(5.12) "In that case, the inclusion of the term 'ascertained' (*niścita*) should not be made.
No, for it serves another purpose.

For those who maintain that a reason is indicative merely by its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), the reason is not at all capable [of proving the conclusion], because it is observed that even when presence and absence exist, the reason may fail to be indicative.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is for the purpose of making it known that the reason (*hetu*) is a signifier precisely through existence and non-existence.
Consequently, the nature of another [thing] does not constitute the definition of the logical mark (*liṅga*),
because the specific characteristics of the mark's own form are not thereby expressed.
For those two, existence and non-existence, are to be understood through the operation of the means of valid cognition that establishes their status, as there is no other means;
for even though the operation of the means of valid cognition establishing them is implied merely by the mention of existence and non-existence, (5.13) [it must be explicitly stated].

Otherwise, the existence of those two alone would be established, because the determination of the existence of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is dependent upon the existence of the cognition (*jñāna*). Thus, in every case, it is precisely the determination of the existence of the object of knowledge that draws forth the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its proof; and since the composition of a treatise is for the sake of others, the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) [is required].

Regarding the term "corroborating" (*saṃvādaka*): since those who have not apprehended that form do not act on its basis, it is established that cognition is the instigator of action precisely because it serves as a characteristic for others.
Nevertheless, some establish those very two—existence and non-existence—as qualified merely by perception and non-perception;
therefore, this word "ascertained" (*niścita*) is employed for the purpose of refuting them.
Even when the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the perception of existence and non-existence are present, there remains doubt;

therefore, it is only through the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) that existence and non-existence are established. For this reason, we have included the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) in order to dispel such misconceptions. Furthermore, since the establishment of the means of cognition that proves [the probans] is achieved merely by stating the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), [the term "ascertained" is necessary].
Cognition does not exist as a separate entity distinct from form,
because it is understood by that very [form],
just like the perception of an object, since it possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva).

(5.14) If it is argued that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are likewise not distinct, because both are understood from the employment of a single [reason], we say: no.
For the presence of the reason in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absence in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) do not imply one another.
It is said that a single statement conveys both [meanings], not that the nature of one thing is the second.

If it is argued: "In the case of the phrase *tatraiva bhāvaḥ* (existence only there), its absence is understood from the fact that it exists as that; and in the case of *atadbhāve 'vaśyamabhāvaḥ* (necessarily non-existence when that is absent), its existence is understood from the fact that it exists as that—thus there is a mutual implication between them."
This statement implies both by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), because even a single indicator of a restriction is inseparable from the implication of the second.
Yet, this does not mean that the two possess a single nature;
their separate mention is for the purpose of restricting their application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, existence and non-existence do not imply one another in isolation;
nor do they do so when restricted, because restriction itself possesses a dual nature.

Therefore, when it is said "existence is in that very [place]," it does not mean that there is existence alone; likewise, by the other term, it is not meant that there is non-existence alone, such that existence or non-existence would imply a second.

Knowledge is not thus [defined], because it is not distinct from the three characteristics [of a valid reason] as understood through knowledge not grasped by treatises that characterize others; therefore, there is no other definition.
Consequently, the reason does not possess six characteristics.
The *Hetubindu*, composed by the Master Dharmakīrti, is completed.
